blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Sparse inertial motion capture typically assumes that each sensor's anatomical identity and mounting orientation are known. We present MOSAIC (Motion-based Sensor Assignment and Inertial Calibration), a framework that recovers this setup from ordinary motion without a calibration pose. Our central insight is that body pose changes continuously while the sensor setup persists, allowing movements that are individually ambiguous to provide complementary evidence over time. A setup network processes unordered sensor streams with temporal and cross-sensor attention, then accumulates assignment and rotation evidence into a session-level estimate. The recovered setup canonicalizes measurements for frozen pretrained pose estimators, separating sensor configuration from motion reconstruction. For sensors worn at prescribed body sites, evaluation on real inertial recordings with randomized setups shows near-calibrated pose accuracy for bounded offsets and substantial benefits from accumulation under arbitrary orientations. Transfer across pose networks supports setup recovery as a reusable interface between interchangeable sensors and pretrained pose models.
blocks.zh: Sparse惯性运动捕捉一般假定每个传感器的解剖特征和上升方向已知. 我们提出MOSAIC(基于运动的传感器任务和惯性校正),这个框架可以从普通运动中恢复这种设置,而不用校正姿势. 我们的核心见解是,在传感器设置持续的同时,身体不断发生变化,使个别模棱两可的移动能够随着时间的推移提供补充证据。 一个设置的网络会处理无序的传感器流,同时注意时间和跨传感器,然后将任务和旋转证据积累到会话级别估计. 被恢复的设置能将被冷冻的预受训练的测量结果作为估计器,将传感器配置与运动重建区分开来. 对于在规定身体场地所穿戴的传感器,对按随机设置进行真实惯性录音的评价显示,接近校正的传感器对有限度的抵消具有精确性,并且从任意取向下的积累中获得了巨大好处。 跨姿势网络的传输支持设置回收,作为可互换传感器和被预训的姿势模型之间的可再用接口.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Sparse inertial motion capture reconstructs full-body movement from a few inertial measurement units (IMUs), supporting animation and motion analysis beyond camera-equipped capture spaces [ 20 , 5 , 12 ] .
Modern systems exploit learned motion priors, kinematic structure and physical constraints to infer joints that are not directly observed [ 24 , 23 , 27 ] .
Their inputs, however, must be associated with the correct body segments and expressed in the expected coordinate frames.
Assigning devices and performing a calibration pose add friction every time the sensors are worn.
Can a user attach interchangeable sensors at the prescribed sites and let ordinary movement recover the setup?

blocks.en:
Our key observation is that setup is persistent even when pose is changing .
Once the devices are attached, different movements provide repeated, complementary observations of the same assignment and mounting rotations.
We propose MOSAIC (Motion-based Sensor Assignment and Inertial Calibration), which exploits this persistence by extracting setup evidence from unordered sensor streams within each motion window and accumulating it over time ( Figs. 1 and 2 ).
Temporal attention captures each stream’s motion and cross-sensor attention relates it to the rest of the body.
Accumulated assignment scores enforce a one-to-one anatomical mapping, and accumulated matrix evidence yields a mounting rotation for each sensor.
The estimate then reorders and aligns the measurements for a frozen pose network.
This separation lets setup evidence span a session while the pose estimator follows the current motion.

blocks.en: The contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: • An online framework that jointly recovers the identities and mounting rotations of six interchangeable IMUs at prescribed sites, without a calibration pose. • A sensor-order-equivariant setup network with persistent evidence accumulation and explicit canonicalization for frozen pose estimators. • An analysis of how motion content and accumulated history determine setup recovery and downstream pose accuracy, including transfer across pretrained pose models.

blocks.en: 2 Related work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
Sparse inertial pose estimation. SIP [ 20 ] fits a body model to six IMUs, and DIP [ 5 ] learns a motion prior for real-time reconstruction.
TransPose [ 24 ] introduces intermediate kinematic predictions and PIP [ 23 ] adds physical constraints. DynaIP [ 27 ] learns velocity and part-specific dynamics.
DiffusionPoser [ 19 ] supports varying sensor configurations and missing measurements through autoregressive diffusion.
These methods address reconstruction from sparse observations.
Our method supplies their required anatomical input convention by estimating the sensor setup before pose inference.

Calibration, assignment and alignment. Static, functional and anatomical calibration use prescribed postures, joint movements or landmarks to identify sensor-to-segment transformations [ 4 , 14 , 13 ] .
TIC [ 31 ] estimates mounting offsets and sensor-specific heading drift during ongoing motion, given known segment identities.
Location recognition from walking [ 6 ] and learned lower-body assignment and alignment [ 30 ] establish that motion can also identify where a sensor is worn.
JointTracker-based calibration [ 17 ] , joint-axis methods [ 15 , 7 ] and RING [ 1 ] exploit kinematic-chain structure to recover alignment or relative orientation.
Our setting combines unknown sensor identities and mounting
rotations at six non-adjacent full-body sites.
We learn relationships across all sensor streams and accumulate
complementary evidence from natural motion to recover a persistent
setup for downstream pose estimation, without requiring a
prescribed calibration pose or motion sequence.

blocks.en: 5 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 5 结论

blocks.en:
We presented MOSAIC for sparse inertial motion capture with unknown
sensor identities and mountings, without a calibration pose.
Accumulating complementary evidence from ordinary motion about the
persistent setup resolves single-window ambiguities and enables pretrained
pose networks to process unfamiliar configurations without retraining.
On real DIP-IMU and TotalCapture recordings, this yields near-calibrated
accuracy under bounded offsets, substantial gains from motion history
under arbitrary orientations, and transfer to PIP and DynaIP.
We further evaluate the framework on real-world IMU recordings that we collected under physical re-attachment, using vision-based pose estimates as a visual reference.

blocks.en:
Each sensor provides 12 input components: its world-frame
free acceleration divided by 30 and its flattened
sensor-to-world orientation matrix.
A shared linear projection maps these inputs to
256-dimensional tokens, followed by a temporal convolution
with kernel size 8, stride 4, and padding 2.
Sinusoidal temporal encodings are added to the resulting
sequence.
Four blocks alternate temporal self-attention within each
stream and cross-sensor self-attention at each time step.
Each layer uses pre-normalization, four attention heads and
a 1024-dimensional feed-forward layer.
After temporal averaging, one additional cross-sensor layer
feeds the assignment and mounting heads described in the
main paper. For arbitrary mountings, a separate linear layer maps
each sensor’s feature after the final cross-sensor layer
to a scalar, followed by softplus to produce the
confidence weight.
